item.title: Why Quitting Drinking Affects Our Relationships
item.description:
Alcoholism

Why Quitting Drinking Affects Our Relationships

The fear of losing friends may be keeping you stuck more than alcohol.

Posted June 21, 2026

“I am afraid I’d lose my friendship if I stopped drinking.”

It’s a fear that I hear a lot when working with people who are considering leaving their old drinking days behind.

How would changing my drinking affect my relationships? This is a legitimate concern many of us have to navigate when trying to leave alcohol behind, especially when we're living in a culture where alcohol has so often become a central part of our social lives. It’s hard not to wonder what impact it would have on our relationships when we choose to no longer participate in the drinking culture. Sometimes, people feel like they have to continue to drink, not because they still love it, but because they are afraid of what they may lose if they stop.

How Major Life Changes Often Filter Our Relationships

So, could letting go of alcohol affect your relationships?

I wish I could tell you it was a myth, that changing our relationship with alcohol will never affect our relationships. But that wouldn't be entirely honest.

The truth is, major life changes often become an inadvertent filter for the relationships in our lives. Whether it is graduating from college, changing jobs, moving cities, or even starting a family, major life changes can reshape our lives. As our priorities shift, some friendships naturally drift apart. The same thing can happen when we choose to leave behind our old drinking days.

Looking back on my own journey, I now see similar loss happening as alcohol first started to take up more space in my life. As drinking-related activities slowly became my preferred way of socializing, distance grew between me and friends who don’t enjoy drinking. I am embarrassed to say that, deep in my love affair with alcohol, I barely noticed the slow drifting apart.

Oftentimes, we worry about what we might lose if we stop drinking, but fail to notice what we may already be losing because of it.

True Connections Often Endure

Realizing that some relationships might fade away may sadden you, but there is a deeper layer of truth: A filter is selective. While it sifts out what no longer fits your current stage of life, it also reveals the relationships that can grow with us through change.

Our relationships are held together by many things. Some are held together by a single thread of commonality: the same ZIP code, the same night classes, the same gym membership, or the same passion for alcohol. Others are held together by something much more durable: shared values, common interests, or love and genuine connection.

While some relationships fade when the single holding thread dissolves, others persevere and deepen through different seasons. From my experience, people with whom we share true connections almost always find ways to remain in our lives even as we grow and change.

How the Stories We Tell Ourselves Keep Us Stuck

Of course, these insights became available to me only after I stepped out of that chapter of my life and looked back. When we are still living it from within, it is only human to focus on what we stand to lose. In doing so, we often lose sight of the fuller picture.

Oftentimes, people mistakenly think that changing one’s relationship with alcohol is all about willpower and discipline. They miss that what keeps pulling a person back to the same drinking pattern is often not alcohol alone, but what alcohol represents or what one may lose if they fully let it go.

The Invisible Drinking Loop
Source: Sober Curiosity

In what I term the Invisible Drinking Loop, I call this a limiting narrative. A limiting narrative is a story we tell ourselves that holds us back or keeps us stuck.

When a limiting narrative like “I will lose all my friends if I quit drinking” is left unnamed and unaddressed, it often becomes an invisible force that keeps us stuck in the same drinking pattern. A part of us wants to grow beyond alcohol, yet a part of us wants to hold on to it so that we don’t “lose everyone we care about.”

The first step of upgrading a limiting narrative is to become aware of the story that we tell ourselves.

Beyond Alcohol: Seeing the Fuller Story

Once you are able to tell the fuller story, you might even be surprised to find that sometimes old relationships find their way back into our lives as the seasons shift.

In the months after alcohol slowly faded out of my life, I found myself reconnecting with friendships that I once neglected as I prioritized alcohol. As laughter was exchanged between us over cups of afternoon tea, it was like time had never passed.

While some of your relationships may change shape as you outgrow your old drinking patterns, you may also discover unexpected joy and connection waiting for you at the other end.

If you would like to understand your relationship with alcohol through a more compassionate lens, you can learn more about the Beyond Alcohol Project on my website.

item.title: Self-Doubt and Negative Judgments
item.description:
Ethics and Morality

Self-Doubt and Negative Judgments

Self-doubt and negative judgments almost always go together.

Posted June 21, 2026

Key points
  • The negative judgments we make about others typically follow suppression of doubt.
  • We swim in an ocean of doubt while judging that we walk on solid ground.
  • Denial of doubt impedes learning and emotional growth.

The negative judgments we make about others typically follow suppression of doubt and often reveal hidden negative self-judgments. We tend to criticize in others what we dislike, fear, or reject within ourselves. Likewise, the contempt we direct outward usually has roots within us.

Whether tacit or conscious, judgments shape our emotional demeanor—body language, facial expressions, tone of voice—and the subtle signals that communicate distrust, disdain, or hostility.

Negative judgments most clearly manifest in the use of negative labels, which create an illusion of certainty for those who use them, even as they provoke hostile responses from others.

No person and no group can be reduced to a label. Negative labels oversimplify, devalue, and slur. They erase complexity and individuality. They weaken relationships, serve as impotent weapons in culture wars, and fill those who use them with contempt. Labels offer the illusion of understanding while preventing genuine understanding. They make it seem like we walk on solid ground when floating on a sea of doubt.

Thinking is hard, that’s why people judge. – Jung.

The Link Between Judgment, Doubt, and Certainty

Genuine conviction is not the absence of doubt but the resolution of known doubt after careful examination of conflicting evidence. Conviction earned through inquiry is strong; a sense of certainty achieved through denial or suppression of doubt is fragile.

Intolerance of doubt obscures what we stand for and makes us focus on what we’re against. Being against something stimulates adrenaline, with temporary boosts of energy and confidence. But a life organized around opposition inevitably gravitates toward condemning those who don't agree with us. Rather than seeking fairness, understanding, or justice, we're preoccupied with exerting power, winning arguments, or exacting retribution. Opposition may feel like conviction, but it typically masks doubt.

Doubt is an uncomfortable condition, but certainty is a ridiculous one. – Voltaire.

We cannot learn anything worth retaining without at least initial doubt. Indeed, science cannot progress without it. Every meaningful discovery begins with questioning assumptions and challenging accepted beliefs. Doubt is not the enemy of knowledge; it’s the engine of knowledge. Suppressing and denying doubt are the primary ways we lie to ourselves.

Surety brings ruin. – Oracle of Delphi.

While doubt is insidious when suppressed or denied, it’s invaluable when it motivates curiosity, learning, and growth.

When doubt motivates learning, it leads to probabilistic thinking and deeper analysis, rather than focus on absolutes or cherry-picked evidence. It reduces—but does not eliminate—confirmation bias. It makes us more willing to consider evidence that challenges our own conclusions. When doubt motivates learning, judgment comes at the end of analysis, not the beginning.

article continues after advertisement

Why Reserving Judgment Is a Lost but Crucial Virtue

Perhaps the most lamentable of lost virtues is the ability to reserve judgment. To reserve judgment is not to abandon values or convictions but to recognize the limits of our knowledge and the complexity of human beings. It is to remain open to learning before deciding, to understand before condemning, and to let doubt perform its essential role in the pursuit of truth.

In an age when every form of media amplifies emotional reactivity, doubt has become increasingly difficult to tolerate. Outrage is rewarded. Seeming certainty is celebrated. Nuance is dismissed as weakness or heresy. Under these conditions, one of the most honest statements a person can make is, "I don't know."

The willingness to say "I don't know" is not a sign of weakness. It is a sign of intellectual honesty. In a culture increasingly obsessed with seeming certainty, intellectual honesty may be one of the highest forms of courage.

item.title: The Long Tail of Disadvantage
item.description:
Resilience

The Long Tail of Disadvantage

Why "just get over it already" is often not that simple.

Posted June 21, 2026

Key points
  • We often imagine disadvantage as a well-defined, single hurdle that is easy to overcome.
  • In reality, disadvantage behaves more like a shadow that stretches far beyond the moments that created it.
  • Progress toward equality takes time due to lingering effects of earlier barriers compounded by new ones.

We often imagine disadvantage as a well-defined hurdle: a single obstacle that appears, is overcome, and then is swiftly forgotten. The implicit story is one of simplicity—a challenge was met, a lesson learned, and a problem solved.

The long shadow.
Source: Celeste Mendoza Nandayapa/Getty Images

Disadvantage and its long shadow

But in reality, disadvantage behaves less like a hurdle and more like a shadow, one that stretches far beyond the moment that created it. Moreover, disadvantage is rarely a single event and more often a series of compounding experiences. Some clearly identifiable, many others crazy-making opaque. Each experience must be navigated, interpreted, and integrated. Over time, these shadows accumulate, not always visibly, not always consciously, but undeniably powerfully. The result is a weight that individuals carry forward, long after any single obstacle has technically been overcome or "forgotten." A very real weight that often at some point starts to colour the lens through which we view the world.

Consider the following:

  • A first-in-family university student enters higher education without insider knowledge, navigating unfamiliar systems while questioning whether they truly belong.
  • A Ph.D. student’s publication record slows during early motherhood, prompting others and the student themselves to question their capability or commitment.
  • An Indigenous surgeon works within institutions not designed with them in mind, while repeatedly encountering suggestions that their success is undeserved.
  • A migrant IT technician, newly arrived from a non-Western country, struggles to access informal networks that often determine who gets their foot in the door.

In each of these cases, it is easy, and often tempting, to attribute difficulties to individual shortcomings: lack of motivation, talent, or resilience. And sure, individual agency does matter. However, a sole focus on the individual obscures something equally, if not more, important: the power of the systems in which we operate and live.

Cumulative disadvantage ripples

Family socioeconomic status, access to networks, caring responsibilities, institutional cultures, and the broader marginalisation of certain groups all shape the opportunities available to us. Barriers continue to influence trajectories in often initially subtle but cumulatively negative ways. Sociologists refer to this as cumulative disadvantage. Early barriers do not vanish once crossed, but instead their effects ripple forward, shaping access to resources, confidence, networks, and opportunities across decades (DiPrete & Eirich, 2006). Often creating vicious cycles of disadvantage.

article continues after advertisement

In this sense, disadvantage has a long, complex tail; it lingers, compounds, and often remains unacknowledged. This matters, not only for how we understand individual lives, but also for how we talk about responsibility. And for how we behave and feel when the solutions to disadvantage are not as quick or immediate as we would like them to be.

Populist narratives often overlook systemic influences

In recent years, many populist narratives have leaned heavily on the language of personal responsibility, often downplaying or simply ignoring structural influences on success and struggle altogether. Some public figures in the U.S. and beyond frequently frame disadvantage as a matter of individual or outgroup failure—not as the product of broader systems of oppression and disadvantage with distributed responsibilities within which individuals operate. Such populist narratives are appealing in their simplicity as they offer clear causes and simple solutions. But they also risk erasing the complex, layered realities of lived experience and real life and hamper real progress towards equality.

Recognising the long tail of disadvantage does not mean dismissing personal agency. Rather, it means situating agency within context. It means acknowledging that success and struggle are rarely the result of a single moment or a single choice, but of cumulative pathways shaped by both individuals and the multi-level environments they inhabit.

We need persistent allies and advocates

When we tell people to "just get over it," we often overlook the shadows they may still be carrying as well as future shadows they very likely will encounter. Unfortunately, a single opportunity, one instance of advocacy, or ‘a foot in the door’ may not be enough to counter the shadow of disadvantage. For allies and advocates, it can sometimes feel frustrating or disheartening when support and advocacy appear to disappear into a void without producing immediate, visible results. Yet this too is part of understanding cumulative disadvantage. Progress may be slow not because individuals have failed to seize opportunities, but because they continue to navigate the lingering effects of earlier barriers and the emergence of new ones. And just because progress is slow does not mean it is not achievable.

article continues after advertisement

Our joint responsibility as individuals and as a society then is not simply to open a door once and expect inequality to resolve itself. It is to recognize the long shadow that disadvantage can cast and to resist interpreting its effects as individual shortcomings. To resist reaching for simplistic populist solutions to complex issues.

item.title: No Spoilers: When Journalists Don't Know the Ending
item.description:
Bias

No Spoilers: When Journalists Don't Know the Ending

Science reporting might be less biased when study results are hidden.

Posted June 21, 2026

Key points
  • Publication bias occurs in academic journals as well as the mainstream media.
  • Recent research suggests that journalists prefer to report on studies with strong methodology.
  • Journalists also exhibit confirmation bias, preferring findings that fit with their preexisting beliefs.

In a 2010 blog post, researcher Michael Inzlicht told the story of the finding that wasn’t. The now-unsupported idea of ego depletion suggested that self-control was limited: You could run out of it if you used up too much. This meant that, for example, if you went to the gym and chose a healthy lunch earlier in the day, both of which required self-control, then you might yell at your spouse later—the reason being that your self-control was depleted. Inzlicht was one of the early researchers of ego depletion, and, as an ethical scientist, he had the courage to accept dissent and speak out when numerous excellent studies didn’t support it (including large meta-analyses). In his words, “the idea that a few minutes of self-control can leave you unable to resist temptation later has been thoroughly debunked.”

In its heyday, though, ego depletion was all the rage. It was heavily covered in the news: As Inzlicht pointed out, even then-President Barack Obama cited it while in office. Why? It’s a splashy finding, and it makes some kind of sense, even though no scientist found a biological mechanism by which it would work. And if we believed the idea of ego depletion, we might just think we spot it in our own lives—confirmation bias in action. We now know that academic journal editors historically preferred exciting findings, particularly in comparison to studies that found no differences—what researchers call null results. And journalists, being people, too, fell for the glamorous findings as well.

The media tend to publish splashy findings that attract clicks and likes. This is a form of publication bias that favors exciting findings over “null results.” Research suggests that science journalists tend to prioritize research with strong methodology, but at times they can succumb to confirmation bias, preferring findings that fit their preexisting beliefs. Research also suggests that confirmation bias is diminished when journalists see summaries of research that omits the findings.
Source: Annor Bright Shem/Pexels

No Spoilers

How do we overcome human nature and get science journalists to be more objective in their choices of what research to cover? A new study by Alexa Tullett and colleagues (2026) explored whether journalists would make different decisions depending on whether they knew a study’s results. 413 journalists, editors, and journalism faculty and graduate students were randomly assigned to one of two groups. Half read traditional summaries of research that included results. Half read what the researchers called “results-blind” summaries that omitted the findings.

Participants in both groups preferred studies with characteristics of good research, including that the study had been preregistered (posted beforehand so that researchers couldn’t zhuzh the results to find what they wanted) and that it replicated (had been repeated by others). (For more on replication, see our posts about baseball cards and experts.) This is good news because it suggests the media publication bias that amplified the ego-depletion research might be waning.

But the study also found that journalists, like all of us, exhibit confirmation bias, a phenomenon where we pay attention to information that fits with our beliefs and ignore information that does not (which we’ve written about in relation to Wordle, overcoming cynicism, zombie facts, and political disagreement). The researchers found that the lack of results tended to reduce journalists’ confirmation bias: That is, those who saw the full summaries tended to prefer results that fit with their preexisting beliefs, whereas those who saw the “results-blind” summaries could not be influenced by that tendency. It’s important to note that the study’s finding is a small effect, but any reduction of bias could be important in an era where journalists are aiming for more objectivity.

Take-Aways

The study’s results offer some suggestions for journalistic best practices (and probably best practices for academic journal editorial teams, too!). Preregistration is important. This is the practice where researchers document their methods before collecting data. Journalists could make decisions on what to cover based on the methodology outlined in preregistration reports and not on the eventual findings. After all, an excellent study that does not support its hypotheses likely tells us more than a poorly designed study with a wow finding.

The challenge is that news cycles move fast and readers don’t generally take the time to understand the intricacies of journalistic decisions. Reporters would have to help audiences understand exactly why a particular study is given media attention, even if the finding seems to fall flat. Over time, increased transparency about journalist decisions on what stories to report could lead to a shift in what news consumers expect.

item.title: A Hybrid Sovereignty Lesson to Learn From Fable’s Shutdown
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

A Hybrid Sovereignty Lesson to Learn From Fable’s Shutdown

Four steps to stop your thinking from subscription dependency.

Posted June 21, 2026

Key points
  • AI dependence risks both national sovereignty and personal cognitive autonomy.
  • Outsourcing thinking to AI erodes critical skills, creating long-term cognitive vulnerability.
  • True AI sovereignty requires individual habits that preserve independent judgment.

Among the most revealing details in the recent Anthropic episode was how ordinary the dependency felt. On June 12, 2026, Anthropic announced that the U.S. government had issued an export-control directive requiring the company to suspend access to its advanced models, Claude Fable 5 and Claude Mythos 5, for foreign nationals, including foreign national employees. Since the company could not reliably separate eligible from ineligible users in real time, it disabled the models for all customers.

Three days earlier, Anthropic had presented Fable 5 as its most capable generally available model, with exceptional performance in software engineering, scientific work, document analysis, and long-horizon reasoning. Mythos 5, a more restricted version, was designed for selected cyber-defenders and infrastructure providers. Within one week, a private company showcased an instrument of extraordinary cognitive and operational power, and a government order interrupted global access to it.

A sovereignty lesson that matters for each of us

We usually imagine sovereignty as a country’s ability to control borders, currency, infrastructure, or law. In an AI-mediated society, sovereignty also includes the capacity to think, judge, learn, remember, and decide without becoming structurally dependent on tools controlled elsewhere. Countries can lose sovereignty when their public institutions, universities, firms, and security systems rely on AI models owned by a handful of companies.

The external dimension of hybrid sovereignty loss

External dependency is visible at ever more places around us. Sovereignty itself is increasingly being sold back to states as a product: sovereign clouds, sovereign models, sovereign data centers. We are witnessing the commodification of sovereignty, and with it the commodification of the very essence of society. And of ourselves?

The word “sovereignty” sounds empowering. The arrangement can still result in paralysis. At the macro level, a country may claim AI sovereignty, yet leave the essential design choices, technical standards, update cycles, and economic terms in private hands. It may be the principal rightsholder of the contract, but de facto it is merely leasing a share stake of a corporate nervous system. And there seem to be few alternatives. The AI sovereignty paradox refers to a state where governments need frontier firms to remain competitive, while those firms can shape the strategic options of governments. That is a remarkable inversion. The state becomes dependent on the corporation’s capability; the corporation becomes vulnerable to the state’s permission; citizens live downstream from both.

The power struggle around AI is not confined to data, chips, or even national security. It reaches into the structure of thought itself. Our minds are at stake.

The internal dimensions of hybrid sovereignty loss

The internal dependency is more intimate. It enters through habits rather than laws. We ask AI to summarize what we have not read, draft what we have not yet thought, decide what matters in a document we have only skimmed, and produce language that sounds like judgment. At first, this feels like efficiency. Over time, the mind may learn a new reflex: reach for the system before reaching inward.

As humans we have evolved to conserve mental energy. We lean on shortcuts, defaults, authority cues, and social proof. Generative AI wraps all four into a conversational surface. It speaks with confidence. It reduces friction. It gives us a polished answer before our own uncertainty has had time to become useful.

That has costs. A Microsoft Research study of 319 knowledge workers found that higher confidence in generative AI was associated with less critical thinking, while stronger self-confidence was associated with more. The issue is subtle. Humans do not stop thinking because they are lazy. They stop thinking at the decisive moment because the tool arrives earlier, cleaner, and with fewer visible hesitations than the human mind.

MIT research adds another caution. A study on AI-assisted news verification, found that participants who relied on AI systems became better at spotting false content in the moment, but then became worse at detecting misinformation on their own when the tool was removed. The finding captures the bargain many of us are making: better performance now, weaker independent capacity later.

By now well known, the MIT-linked preprint, "Your Brain on ChatGPT," used EEG measures during essay writing and reported lower neural connectivity and weaker ownership among participants using an LLM compared with those writing without tools. The study had methodological limits and attracted criticism, including a comment urging conservative interpretation. Yet even with those caveats, the concern it raised is legitimate. We are experimenting with cognition at population scale, often without naming the experiment.

The danger is not that AI helps us

The danger is that our artificial assets are becoming part of the architecture within which our mind evolves. A calculator does not tell us what is worth calculating. A navigation app does not rewrite our values. Whereas a generative AI system can shape the problem, supply both the options—and the opinion regarding those options, polish the reasoning, soften the discomfort, and deliver the final words. It can become a cognitive environment, not just a tool. That’s when hybrid sovereignty loss shows its dark personal side.

That is why the Anthropic episode matters beyond Anthropic. It shows how dependency accumulates across layers. At the geopolitical level, countries may discover that critical capacities sit in privately owned systems subject to foreign law, corporate incentives, and sudden access changes. At the institutional level, organizations may redesign work around tools they cannot inspect, repair, or replace quickly. At the personal level, individuals may trade the messiness of their own thinking for the smoothness of outsourced cognition.

The result is a hollowing out of sovereignty from both ends. Externally, societies outsource strategic capacity. Internally, humans outsource the small acts of attention from which judgment is built. The first loss appears in policy. The second appears in behavior: less patience with ambiguity, less confidence in one’s own first draft, less tolerance for the slow work of forming a view.

A healthier relationship with AI requires a new discipline of use. We need tools that strengthen our own agency, and institutions that treat human thinking as a skill that needs exercise. AI can extend the mind. It can also domesticate it. The difference lies in the habits we build now.

AUTOS: A Practical Takeaway to See and Stop Internal Sovereignty Loss

A — Attend first. Before asking AI, write down your own question, assumption, or first answer. Give your mind a starting position. Note when this is becoming hard.

U — Use deliberately. Assign AI a role: critic, tutor, summarizer, translator, challenger. Avoid open-ended delegation when judgment matters. Push yourself to pause and think.

T — Trace the source. Ask where claims come from. Check original evidence, especially for health, law, politics, finance, and science. Avoid the path of least resistance, and notice when you are tempted to take it.

O — Own the conclusion. Never publish, forward, decide, or advise with words you cannot defend as your own.

S — Strengthen your own sovereignty. Build regular AI-free zones for reading, writing, planning, remembering, and deciding. You are still the master of your own mind; the less you exert that power the easier you become to steer by others, and algorithms.

The future of sovereignty will be written in treaties, procurement rules, and compute infrastructure. It will also be written in the private moment before we click “ask.” That is where dependency begins. That is also where agency can return. Hybrid sovereignty starts inside.
